analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigned a MALWARE prediction with probability 0.8033, but the supplied evidence is weak and mostly non-specific. Of the Top-20 n-grams, 16 have a relative frequency of 0.000000, so their positive SHAP contributions (CMOVZ MOV +0.014673, ADD POP +0.013845, XOR XOR +0.012564, PUSH SUB +0.011626, CALL ADD +0.009473, XOR CALL +0.009321, MOV JZ +0.007985, CMP CMOVZ +0.007787, TEST JZ +0.007434, TEST JS +0.007103, XOR SHL +0.007053, SUB MOV +0.006983, AND MOV +0.006792, CMP JL +0.006299, LEA CALL +0.006256) reflect the model treating the absence of these patterns as pushing toward the malware class. They are not observed instruction sequences, so they cannot be cited as direct evidence of mining behavior. Only a few n-grams are present: MOV PUSH (0.036585, +0.013134) and XOR PUSH (0.012195, +0.007364) lean toward cryptojacking, while XOR MOV (0.024390, -0.014976), XOR TEST (0.012195, -0.010016) and MOV XOR (0.024390, -0.007473) lean benign. MOV PUSH and XOR PUSH are generic stack and register setup patterns common in ordinary compiled code. The one distinctive crypto-like pattern in the list, XOR SHL, has zero frequency, and no function-level locations are given for any n-gram. There is therefore no observed hashing, bit-rotation, or tight-loop arithmetic evidence. The high model probability comes mainly from absent features, which is inconclusive and does not support a high-confidence call. Because the observed benign-leaning features offset part of the observed malware-leaning ones, and the model score is still fairly high, the result is low-confidence.

analysis.recommended_action: Treat as inconclusive and do not label as cryptojacking on this evidence alone. Perform further analysis, including disassembly of the binary to look for actual hashing or bit-rotation loops, review of imports and strings, and sandbox behavioral monitoring (CPU usage, network connections to mining pools). Also check the sample against threat intelligence and known-malware hash databases.
